import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt



dataset_raw = pd.read_excel("./spiderman.xlsx")
dataset_raw.columns = ["Elements"] + list(dataset_raw.columns[1:])
dataset_raw



sample_names = pd.read_excel("./spiderman.xlsx", index_col=0, header=None)
name_row = sample_names.iloc[0,:].reset_index(drop=True)
name_row



spdr_elements = [
    "Cs", "Rb", "Ba", "Th", "U", "Nb", "Ta", "K", 
    "La", "Ce", "Pb", "Sr", "P", "Nd", "Sm", "Zr", 
    "Hf", "Eu", "Ti", "Tb", "Y", "Yb", "Lu"
]



dataset = dataset_raw[dataset_raw["Elements"].isin(spdr_elements)]
dataset = dataset.set_index("Elements")
dataset = dataset.reindex(spdr_elements)
dataset = dataset.reset_index()
dataset



reference = pd.read_excel("./reference.xlsx")
reference



normalised_dataset = []

for i in range(1, dataset.columns.size):
    calculated = dataset.iloc[:, i] / reference["Primitive Mantle"]
    normalised_dataset.append(calculated)



normalised_df = pd.DataFrame(normalised_dataset).transpose()
normalised_df



reference



for i in range(normalised_df.columns.size):
    plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
    plt.plot(dataset["Elements"], normalised_df[i], label=f"{name_row[i]}")
    plt.plot(dataset["Elements"], reference["OIB"], color="green", label="OIB") #OIB
    plt.title(f"sample name: {name_row[i]}")
    plt.yscale('log')
    plt.ylim(1e0,1e3)
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()





















# Create a 2x5 grid of subplots
fig, axes = plt.subplots(5, 2, figsize=(12.5, 17.5))

# Flatten the axes array to make it easier to loop through
axes = axes.flatten()

# Loop through the columns and plot on each subplot
for i in range(normalised_df.columns.size):
    ax = axes[i]  # Get the axis for the current plot
    ax.plot(dataset["Elements"], normalised_df[i], label=f"{name_row[i]}")
    ax.plot(dataset["Elements"], reference["OIB"], color="green", label="OIB") #OIB
    ax.set_title(f"sample name: {name_row[i]}")
    ax.set_yscale('log')
    ax.set_ylim(1e0, 1e3)
    ax.legend()

# Adjust layout to avoid overlap
plt.tight_layout()

# Show the plot
plt.show()



plt.figure(figsize=(10.5,6))

plt.plot(dataset["Elements"], reference["OIB"], color="black", label="OIB", linewidth=3) #OIB

The temperature-dependent oxygen isotope fractionation between Opx and Cpx is given by:\Delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} = \delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx}} - \delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Cpx}}

where:

\Delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} is the fractionation (‰)

\delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx}} and \delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Cpx}} are the isotope values of the minerals.
The fractionation factor \alpha relates to temperature (T in Kelvin):1000 \ln \alpha_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} = \frac{A \times 10^6}{T^2} + B

Matthews et al. (1983):1000 \ln \alpha_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} = \frac{1.88 \times 10^6}{T^2} - 3.13

Chiba et al. (1989) (recommended):1000 \ln \alpha_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} = \frac{1.57 \times 10^6}{T^2} - 0.53

Rearranging the Chiba et al. (1989) equation:T(K) = \sqrt{\frac{1.57 \times 10^6}{\Delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} + 0.53}}

Convert to °C:T(°C) = T(K) - 273.15

Given:

\delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx}} = 5.6\ ‰

\delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Cpx}} = 5.2\ ‰

Calculate \Delta^{18}\text{O}:\Delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{Opx-Cpx}} = 5.6 - 5.2 = 0.4\ ‰

Compute temperature (Chiba calibration):T(K) = \sqrt{\frac{1.57 \times 10^6}{0.4 + 0.53}} = \sqrt{1.688 \times 10^6} \approx 1298\ \text{K}

Convert to °C:T(°C) = 1298 - 273.15 \approx 1025°C

Result: Crystallization temperature ≈ 1025°C.

import numpy as np

def calculate_opx_cpx_temp(d18O_opx: float, d18O_cpx: float, calibration: str = "Chiba") -> float:
    """
    Calculate crystallization temperature using Opx-Cpx δ¹⁸O fractionation.
    
    Parameters:
        d18O_opx (float): δ¹⁸O of orthopyroxene (‰).
        d18O_cpx (float): δ¹⁸O of clinopyroxene (‰).
        calibration (str): "Chiba" (default) or "Matthews".
    
    Returns:
        Temperature in °C.
    """
    delta = d18O_opx - d18O_cpx
    
    if calibration == "Chiba":
        A, B = 1.57e6, 0.53
    elif calibration == "Matthews":
        A, B = 1.88e6, 3.13
    else:
        raise ValueError("Calibration must be 'Chiba' or 'Matthews'.")
    
    T_kelvin = np.sqrt(A / (delta + B))
    T_celsius = T_kelvin - 273.15
    
    return T_celsius



# Example usage
d18O_opx = 6.621231   # ‰
d18O_cpx = 6.225780   # ‰
temp = calculate_opx_cpx_temp(d18O_opx, d18O_cpx, calibration="Chiba")
print(f"Calculated Temperature: {temp:.1f}°C")

In triple oxygen isotope geochemistry, we often use the linearized form of delta notation.

This is called delta-prime notation:\delta'^{x}\mathrm{O}
=
1000
\ln
\left(
1+
\frac{\delta^{x}\mathrm{O}}{1000}
\right)

where x can be 17 or 18.

Therefore:\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
=
1000
\ln
\left(
1+
\frac{\delta^{17}\mathrm{O}}{1000}
\right)

and\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}
=
1000
\ln
\left(
1+
\frac{\delta^{18}\mathrm{O}}{1000}
\right)

For small isotope variations, \delta and \delta' are very similar.

However, \delta' is mathematically useful because isotope fractionation becomes additive in logarithmic space.

In mass-dependent fractionation, ^{17}\mathrm{O} and ^{18}\mathrm{O} usually vary together.

Because ^{17}\mathrm{O} is intermediate in mass between ^{16}\mathrm{O} and ^{18}\mathrm{O}, the change in \delta^{17}\mathrm{O} is approximately about half of the change in \delta^{18}\mathrm{O}.

In linearized notation, this relationship is commonly written as:\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
=
\lambda
\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}
+
\gamma

where:

\lambda is the slope of the reference line

\gamma is the intercept

\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} and \delta'^{18}\mathrm{O} are the linearized isotope values

A commonly used simplified form is:\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
=
\lambda
\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}

with, for example:\lambda = 0.528

This line represents the expected mass-dependent relationship between ^{17}\mathrm{O} and ^{18}\mathrm{O}.

The parameter \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} describes the deviation of a sample from a chosen mass-dependent reference line.

It is commonly defined as:\Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
=
\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
-
\lambda
\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}

where \lambda is the chosen reference slope.

If the reference line includes an intercept, the equation becomes:\Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
=
\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
-
\left(
\lambda
\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}
+
\gamma
\right)

If \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} = 0, the sample lies exactly on the chosen reference line.

If \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} > 0, the sample lies above the reference line.

If \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} < 0, the sample lies below the reference line.

Because \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} values are usually very small, they are often reported in per meg:\Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}_{\mathrm{per\ meg}}
=
1000
\left[
\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
-
\lambda
\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}
\right]

Here, \delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} and \delta'^{18}\mathrm{O} are in per mil, while \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}_{\mathrm{per\ meg}} is in per meg.

In triple oxygen isotope geochemistry, both \theta and \lambda describe slopes in oxygen isotope space, but they are often used differently.

The exponent \theta is commonly used for a specific fractionation process between two phases:\theta_{A-B}
=
\frac{
\ln \alpha^{17}_{A-B}
}{
\ln \alpha^{18}_{A-B}
}

For example, \theta may describe equilibrium fractionation between quartz and water, or another specific mineral-fluid pair.

The parameter \lambda is commonly used for a reference line or empirical relationship in isotope space:\delta'^{17}\mathrm{O}
=
\lambda
\delta'^{18}\mathrm{O}
+
\gamma

In simple terms:

\theta describes the slope of a specific fractionation process.

\lambda describes the slope of a chosen reference line.

Because \Delta'^{17}\mathrm{O} depends on the chosen reference slope, the value of \lambda should always be reported.

The isotopic ratio of the mixture is given by:\left( \frac{^{87}\text{Sr}}{^{86}\text{Sr}} \right)_{\text{mix}} = \frac{[\text{Sr}]_A \cdot \left( \frac{^{87}\text{Sr}}{^{86}\text{Sr}} \right)_A \cdot (1 - x) + [\text{Sr}]_B \cdot \left( \frac{^{87}\text{Sr}}{^{86}\text{Sr}} \right)_B \cdot x \cdot r}{[\text{Sr}]_A \cdot (1 - x) + [\text{Sr}]_B \cdot x \cdot r}

Where:

[\text{Sr}]_A, [\text{Sr}]_B = Sr concentrations in end-members A (mantle) and B (crust)

r = \frac{[\text{Sr}]_B}{[\text{Sr}]_A} = concentration ratio (5:1, 1:10, etc.)

x = mixing fraction (0 to 1)\delta^{18}\text{O}_{\text{mix}} = \delta^{18}\text{O}_A (1 - x) + \delta^{18}\text{O}_B \cdot x \ \ \text{(linear mixing for oxygen)}

def epsilon_nd(nd_143_144_sample):
    # CHUR reference value for 143Nd/144Nd
    nd_143_144_chur = 0.512638

    # εNd
    epsilon_nd = ((nd_143_144_sample / nd_143_144_chur) - 1) * 10**4

    return epsilon_nd
